lesson.title: Collapsing a Network Into One Number: Equivalent Resistance
lesson.summary: Equivalent resistance is the single resistor value that would draw the same current from the same source as an entire network, found by repeatedly combining series and parallel groups.
lesson.body:
Equivalent resistance, sometimes called total resistance, is the single resistor value that would behave identically, from the outside, to an entire network of resistors. If you replaced the whole tangle of components with just that one resistor, a source connected to the terminals would draw exactly the same current and see exactly the same voltage. This matters because it lets you analyze a complicated network's overall behavior using nothing more than plain Ohm's law, while still being able to work backward into the network to find individual branch currents when you need them.

Finding an equivalent resistance almost always comes down to two combining rules used over and over: resistors in series simply add, R_series = R1 + R2 + ..., and resistors in parallel combine by reciprocals, 1 divided by R_parallel equals 1 divided by R1 plus 1 divided by R2, and so on. Most networks can be reduced entirely by spotting series and parallel groups, replacing each with its single equivalent value, and repeating until only one resistor remains.

Take a network with R1 = 2 ohm in series with a parallel pair of R2 = 6 ohm and R3 = 3 ohm. Combine the parallel pair first: (6 times 3) divided by (6 plus 3), which is 18 divided by 9, or 2 ohm. Now that parallel combination behaves as a single 2 ohm resistor in series with R1, so the total equivalent resistance is 2 ohm plus 2 ohm, or 4 ohm.

That single number tells you everything about how the network behaves from a source's point of view. If an 8V source is connected across the whole network, the total current is I = 8V divided by 4 ohm, or 2A, exactly as if a lone 4 ohm resistor were there. Working backward, the voltage across the parallel section is I times its 2 ohm equivalent, or 4V, which then splits into branch currents of 4V divided by 6 ohm, about 0.667A through R2, and 4V divided by 3 ohm, about 1.333A through R3. Those two branch currents add back up to 2A, confirming the reduction was done correctly.

Series and parallel reduction handles most practical networks, but it has a real limit: some networks, the classic example being a bridge circuit with a resistor connected diagonally across the middle, have no pair of resistors that is purely in series or purely in parallel with anything else. When you get stuck that way, plain equivalent resistance reduction cannot finish the job on its own, and you need an additional tool, the delta wye transformation covered soon, to unlock the rest of the network. Equivalent resistance is nonetheless the foundation everything else rests on: it is what makes Thevenin reduction possible, what a load resistance calculation ultimately measures against, and the last step of any full circuit simplification, no matter how many extra tools were needed to get there.

It also pays to check a reduction against two sanity habits before trusting it. First, the equivalent resistance of resistors purely in series can never be smaller than the largest individual resistor, since every added resistor only adds more opposition to current. Second, the equivalent resistance of resistors purely in parallel can never be larger than the smallest individual resistor, since adding another path can only give current more ways to flow, never fewer. In the worked example above, the parallel pair reduced from 6 ohm and 3 ohm down to 2 ohm, smaller than either original value, and the final series total of 4 ohm is larger than either the 2 ohm resistor or the 2 ohm equivalent it was added to, both exactly as those two rules predict.
